en: *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, one fascicle.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.

The Mahāyāna establishes that the three realms are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), because the sūtras state that the three realms are mind-only (*cittamātra*); "mind" (*citta*), "intellect" (*manas*), "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), and "cognition" (*vijñapti*) are merely different names for the same thing.

In this context, "mind" (*citta*) is mentioned, while "mental faculty" (*manas*) includes mental factors (*caitta*). This serves only to exclude external objects and does not negate the associated [factors]. When internal consciousness arises, it manifests as if it were an external object, just as one with cataracts sees hairs, flies, and the like; herein, there is not even the slightest bit of real meaning.
Regarding this very point, an objection is raised.
The verse says:
If consciousness lacks a real object, then there would be no determination of place and time.
If the continuity [of the agent] were not determinate, its activity could not be established.
The treatise asks:
What is the meaning of this statement?

If there were truly external dharmas such as form apart from consciousness, and the consciousnesses of form and so forth arose without taking form and so forth as their objects, for what reason would this consciousness arise in certain locations and not in all locations?
Why is it that consciousness arises at this location only at certain times and not at all times?
Furthermore, since there are many continuums in the same place at the same time, why is it not determined that any one of them gives rise to consciousness?
Just as a person with cataracts sees hairs, flies, and so forth, yet this cognition does not arise in the absence of cataracts—what further reason is there [to claim that objects do not exist]?

For what reason do the hairs and such seen by those with cataracts lack the function of hair and so forth; why do the food, drink, swords, staves, poisons, clothes, and so forth obtained in dreams lack the functions of being drunk and so forth; and why do the city of gandharvas and the like lack the functions of a city and so forth?

Other objects such as hair and the like do have their utility; if they were truly non-existent in the same way that external objects like form and so forth are, and if there were only internal consciousness arising in the semblance of external objects, then fixed locations, fixed times, non-universal continuity, and functional efficacy would all be impossible to establish.
It is not the case that none are established at all.
The verse says:
Place and time are fixed, as in a dream; The body is not fixed, as with hungry ghosts.
"Similarly, one sees rivers of pus and the like; like a dream, they impair what is useful.
The Commentary says:

This is explained according to the meaning of "like a dream," referring to what is seen within a dream. That is to say, although there is no real object in a dream, one may see things such as villages, gardens, men, and women in certain places, but not in all places.
In that very place, one may at times perceive such things as villages or gardens, yet not at all times.
For this reason, although there is no real object external to consciousness, the determination of place and time is nonetheless established.
The phrase "speaking like the speech of ghosts" clarifies that it is like [the world of] hungry ghosts (*preta*).
It is called a "river of pus" because it is filled with pus, just as one speaks of a "butter jar" when it is full of butter.

This means that through the common karmic maturation (*vipāka*) of their shared karma, many hungry ghosts gather together and all perceive the river of pus; it is not the case that only one person perceives it within this [river].
The word "etc. indicates that one may see excrement and so forth, as well as sentient beings wielding swords and staves who block and guard it, preventing others from eating it.
Thus, although there is no real object apart from consciousness, the principle of multiple continua with indeterminate objects is established.
Furthermore, just as objects in a dream lack reality yet still perform functions such as the loss of semen and blood,
so too, although there are no real objects apart from consciousness, the meaning of their illusory activity is established.
Thus, by means of these various individual analogies, it has been demonstrated that the four points—such as the determination of location and so forth—are established.
Furthermore, the verse says:
All are like those in hell, Seeing the same wardens and such.
Because they are capable of causing affliction and harm, all four meanings are established.
The treatise says:
It should be understood that herein, the analogy of a single hell illustrates that all [the other characteristics], such as the fixed location, are likewise established.
The term "hell" indicates those classes of sentient beings who experience the suffering of oppression and harm while dwelling in hell.

This means that although within the hells there are no actual entities such as hell-wardens included among the category of sentient beings, nevertheless, through the predominant power of the karmic maturation of their shared actions, many individual continua—occupying the same place at the same time—all collectively perceive the arrival of hell-wardens, dogs, crows, iron mountains, and other such objects, which perform acts of oppression and harm toward them.
Thus, although there is no real object apart from consciousness, the four points—such as the fixed location [of hell] and so forth—are all established.
For what reason do you not admit that the wardens of hell and the like are actual sentient beings?
Because it is not logical:
first, this [state] should not be subsumed under the hells (*naraka*), for one does not undergo the sufferings experienced there;
furthermore, since they mutually oppress and harm one another, that [state] should not be established as a hell.

Since these hell-wardens and others are equal in form, strength, and power, they should not be excessively terrified of one another; nor should they themselves be unable to endure the suffering of being constantly scorched by the fierce flames and heat of the iron ground. How then could they inflict such torment upon others?

It is not that those who do not belong to the hells should be born there; yet, since animals are actually found in the heavens, the same applies to the hells, where animals and hungry ghosts exist as hell-wardens and the like.
This defense is not tenable.
The verse says:
"As [the case of] animals in the heavens, it is not so within the hells."
Regarding the claim that animals and hungry ghosts are born there [in hell], it is because they do not experience those sufferings.
The treatise says:

Those who are born as animals in the heavens must possess karma capable of inducing the pleasure of that environment; being born there, they certainly experience the pleasure produced by that environment. However, the hell-wardens and others do not experience the suffering produced by the environment within hell; therefore, one should not admit that the destinies of animals and hungry ghosts can be born in the hells (*naraka*).

If that were so, one must admit that through the predominant power of the karma of those hell-beings, distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arise, giving rise to superior distinctions in shape, color, and magnitude; it is upon these that the designation "hell-wardens" is applied. To produce terror in those beings, they manifest various differentiated actions such as moving their hands and feet—like the mountain of rams sometimes separating and sometimes joining, or the thorns of the iron forest sometimes lowering and sometimes raising.
It is not that such a thing is entirely non-existent; however, it would be unreasonable.
The verse says:
"If it is admitted that, by the power of karma, distinct primary elements arise,"
If such a transformation occurs, why do you not allow it to occur in consciousness?
The treatise says:
For what reason do you not allow that consciousness undergoes such a transformation through the power of karma, yet instead maintain that it is the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which do so?
Furthermore, the verse says:
If the perfuming of karma occurs in one place, yet one clings to the fruit as existing in another,
why do you not admit that the consciousness which is perfumed possesses the fruit?
The treatise says:

You maintain that the various transformations of form and so forth in the hells arise from the power of one's own karma, which gives rise to distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*). It stands to reason that the latencies (*vāsanā*) of that karma must be admitted to reside within the continuum of consciousness, not elsewhere. Since you do not admit that there is a transformation of the fruit where there is no latency, yet you instead insist that the fruit exists [in the external elements], what is the reason for this?

If it is argued that scriptural teaching serves as the reason— namely, that if there were only consciousness appearing as form and so forth without any distinct form and so forth, the Buddha would not have spoken of the existence of the sense-bases of form and so forth—
this teaching does not constitute a valid reason, because it possesses a different underlying intention.
The verse says:
Based on those beings to be converted, the World-Honored One, with intentional meaning,
taught that there are bases such as form, just like beings born by transformation.
The treatise says:

As the Buddha taught that there are beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*), he spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) based solely on the fact that the mental continuum (*citta-saṃtati*) proceeds uninterruptedly into future lives; he did not say that beings born by transformation exist as substantial entities.
It is taught that there are no sentient beings or selves, but only the causes of phenomena; therefore, the sense bases such as form are spoken of.

The sūtras are likewise: they speak with intentional meaning (saṃdhāya) based on what is appropriate for those to be converted to receive the teaching, rather than [asserting] that these exist as separate, real entities.
With what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) were the ten [categories], such as form (*rūpa*), taught?
The verse says:
"Consciousness arises from its own seeds and evolves appearing in the likeness of an object."
To establish the internal and external bases (*āyatana*), the Buddha taught them as ten.
The commentary asks:
what is the meaning of this statement?

The consciousness that appears as form arises from the transformation of its own seeds through the convergence of conditions; the Buddha, based on those seeds and the forms they manifest, respectively designates them as the sense-base of the eye and the sense-base of form.

In this manner, up to the manifest consciousness resembling touch, which arises from the transformation of its own seeds through the convergence of conditions, the Buddha—relying on those seeds and the touch that is manifested—designates them respectively as the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) and the touch-base (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
Based on this underlying intention (*saṃdhi*), the ten [categories] beginning with form (*rūpa*) are taught.
What is the benefit of this intentional teaching?
The verse says:
Relying on this teaching, one enters into the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*);
then, relying on further teachings, one enters into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) regarding the objects of apprehension.
The Commentary says:
Based on this teaching of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), those who are to be trained are able to enter into the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

That is to say, if one understands that the six consciousnesses arise from the six pairs of factors, and that there is absolutely no seer up to no knower, then those who are to receive the teaching on the selflessness of sentient beings will be able to realize the selflessness of sentient beings.

Furthermore, based on this, another teaching of Vijñaptimātra is expounded so that those to be converted may enter into the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) as they are grasped.

That is to say, if one understands that what appears as consciousness arises resembling phenomena such as form, and that within this there are no phenomena possessing the characteristics of form and so forth, then those who are to receive the teaching of the selflessness of all phenomena will be able to penetrate the selflessness of phenomena.

If one were to know that all phenomena (*dharma*) are in every respect without entry into selflessness (*anātman*), then even consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) would ultimately be non-existent; what, then, could be established?

It is not by knowing that all phenomena are in every respect non-existent that one is said to have "entered" the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). Rather, it is by realizing that the various phenomena—which are the conceptualized nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) falsely imagined by the ignorant—are without self, that one is said to have entered the selflessness of phenomena. It is not because the ineffable nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which is the domain of the Buddhas, is also entirely non-existent that it is called the selflessness of phenomena.

The nature of this consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā), which is grasped by other consciousnesses, is likewise non-existent in essence; this is called the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya).

Otherwise, if the objects grasped by other consciousnesses were existent, the principle of consciousness-only could not be established, for one would have to admit that those other consciousnesses possess real objects.

By this principle, the teaching of Vijñapti-mātra is established in order to cause all beings universally to realize the selflessness of all phenomena; it is not because it negates existence in every respect.

Furthermore, how is it known that the Buddha spoke with such an underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) regarding the existence of the sense-bases (*āyatana*) such as form, rather than asserting that there are separate, real external dharmas such as form that serve as the respective objects for the consciousnesses of form and so forth?
The verse says:
Because that object is neither a single [entity], nor many atoms, nor their aggregation, and so forth; for the atom itself is not established.
The treatise says:
What is being stated here?

It means that if external bases such as form existed substantially and served as distinct objects for their respective consciousnesses of form and so forth, then such external objects would either have to be a single entity, like the "composite form" (*avayavin*) asserted by the Vaiśeṣikas.

Alternatively, it should be many, as when one maintains that numerous real atoms (*paramāṇu*) exist individually as objects; or it should be a combination and aggregation of many atoms, as when one maintains that numerous real atoms exist together in combination and aggregation as the object.
Furthermore, those external objects should logically not be a single entity, because a composite material body that is distinct from its constituent parts cannot be perceived.
Nor can they logically be many, because individual atoms, being discrete, cannot be perceived.
Furthermore, it is not logical for [the object] to be either a composite or a collection as its objective referent, because the theory of a single, substantial atom is untenable.
Why is it untenable?
The verse says:
If an atom were to join with the six [directions], it would necessarily consist of six parts;
if it were to occupy the same location as the six, then a composite aggregate would be identical to a single atom.
The treatise says:
If a single atom were to combine with one atom in each of the six directions, it would necessarily consist of six parts, because one location cannot simultaneously accommodate another.

If there were six atoms in the space occupied by a single atom, then all composite matter would have to be the same size as a single atom; since they could not exceed that measure relative to one another, composite matter would likewise be invisible.
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīra say:
"Individual atoms do not possess the property of mutual conjunction, because they lack spatial dimensions; thus, the aforementioned fault is avoided.
However, it is only composite matter that possesses the property of conjunction, because it does have spatial dimensions."
This is also not the case.
The verse says:
Since atoms have no conjunction, who is it that possesses conjunction in the aggregate?
"Or else, their conjunction would not be established, not because they lack spatial parts.
The treatise says:
One should now interrogate the logical principle stated by that [opponent].
Since it is distinct from atoms, there is no separate aggregated matter; if atoms do not conjoin, what is it that aggregates?
If one attempts to defend this by saying:
"Aggregated matter, in its successive states, likewise lacks the sense of conjunction."
Then one should not say:
"An atom has no conjunction because it lacks spatial parts," for if an aggregate possesses spatial parts, conjunction is likewise not admitted.
Therefore, atoms do not combine not because they lack spatial parts;
thus, a single, real atom is not established.
Furthermore, even granting that atoms may or may not combine, the faults [of such a position] remain as they are.
If one were to concede that atoms possess parts or are partless, both positions would constitute grave errors. Why is this so?
The verse says:
If atoms possess spatial dimensions, logically they cannot be unitary;
if they lack them, there would be no shadow or obstruction, and an aggregate would not differ from a non-dual [atom].
The treatise says:
If a single atom has multiple parts distinguished by the six directions as its substance, how can it be a unity?
If a single atom had no distinct directional parts, when the sun’s orb just rises and its light touches it, how could a shadow appear on its other side?
Because they lack parts, light cannot reach them.
Furthermore, if one maintains that atoms have no spatial divisions, how could this atom and that atom obstruct each other?
Since there are no parts through which another atom could pass, it can be said that they mutually impede one another.

Since they do not obstruct one another, all atoms would have to occupy the same location; consequently, all material aggregates would be the size of a single atom, leading to the same faults previously mentioned.
Why, then, do you not allow that shadow and obstruction belong to the aggregate and not to the individual atom?
Is it not the case that you admit that an aggregate of atoms (*paramāṇu*) possesses material form (*rūpa*) capable of casting a shadow and acting as an obstruction?
It is not so; for if that were the case, the aggregate would lack duality.
That is to say, if the aggregate-form were not distinct from the atoms, then the shadow and the obstruction would logically fail to belong to the aggregate-form.

Whether one establishes the atom (*paramāṇu*) based on spatial arrangement or as a collection (*saṃghāta*), neither is a single, real entity. What is the use of investigating whether it is an atom or a collection?
One has still not refuted the characteristics of external form (*rūpa*) and so forth; what, then, are these characteristics?
It should be carefully considered together whether the objective spheres of the eye and so forth—which are also the actual nature of blue and so forth—are unitary or manifold.
What is the actual nature of blue and so forth within these objective spheres of the eye and so forth? Is it one or many?
If that were the case, what would be the fault?
Both positions would be erroneous, with many faults as previously described;
moreover, even the first [position] is irrational.
The verse says:
First, there would be no sequential movement; second, [the senses] would reach and not reach simultaneously;
third, there would be many intervening objects; and fourth, subtle things would be difficult to perceive.
The treatise says:

If there were no spatial distinctions, then all objects of the eye such as blue and so forth would be grasped as a single entity, and there would be no gradual progression across a vast terrain, because taking a single step would reach everything.
Furthermore, there would simultaneously be both reaching and not reaching this and that;
for it is logically impossible for a single entity at one time to both obtain and not obtain [a location].

Moreover, in a single spatial location, there should not be the occurrence of multiple elephants, horses, and so forth with intervals between them; if a place occupied by one were identical to that occupied by another, how could one distinguish between "this" and "that"?
Furthermore, how could two [atoms] occupy the same location while one reaches it and the other does not, such that an empty space would be seen between them?

Moreover, there should be no such things as tiny aquatic insects or other subtle objects difficult to perceive, because they would have to be equal in dimension to gross objects if they occupied the same locus.

If it is claimed that this and that distinction constitutes a distinct entity by virtue of its characteristics alone, and not through any other principle, then one must necessarily admit that these distinct entities, when analyzed further and further, resolve into multiple atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Since it has already been demonstrated that an atom is not a single, real substance, then apart from consciousness, neither the eyes and so forth nor forms and so forth—whether as faculties (*indriya*) or as objects (*viṣaya*)—can be established at all.
By this, the principle that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) is well established.
The existence or non-existence of all phenomena is determined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and among all forms of valid cognition, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is supreme.
If external objects did not exist, how could this awareness arise?
"Is it that I have now directly realized such an object?
This realization is not established.
The verse says:
When one realizes that appearances are like dreams and so forth, at the time such realization has arisen, both the seeing and the object have already ceased to exist;
how, then, can you allow for the existence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
The treatise says:

Just as during dreams and the like, although external objects do not exist, such manifest cognitions nevertheless occur, one should know that manifest cognitions at other times are likewise [without external objects]; therefore, their citation of this as proof is unestablished.
Furthermore, if at that time there were such a manifest awareness as "I now directly realize such form and so forth," then at that moment the capacity to see the object would already be absent;

this is because it must be the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that performs the discrimination, and by that time the visual consciousness and the other sensory consciousnesses have necessarily already ceased.

For one who maintains the theory of momentariness (*kṣaṇavāda*), at the time this cognition arises, the manifest objects such as form have already ceased. How, then, can direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) be admitted at that time?

It must be that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has previously experienced them and is now able to recollect; therefore, it is certain that there was an object previously experienced. Since the one who perceives this object is admitted to possess direct perception, the reality of external objects is thereby established.
Thus, the argument that external objects exist must be proven by first perceiving them and subsequently recollecting them;
this reasoning is also untenable.
Why? The verse says:
As it is said: "From the cognition that appears as an object, recollection arises from this.
The commentary states:

As previously explained, although there is no external object, visual consciousness and the like appear as if they were external objects. Subsequently, in a later stage associated with mindfulness, the conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) appears as the prior object; this is precisely what is called "recalling what was previously experienced. Therefore, the argument that one can prove the real existence of an external object through later recollection of what was previously seen is logically untenable.
If, as in a dream, consciousness can arise even though there is no real object, it is the same upon waking.
Just as one naturally knows for oneself during the world that dream-objects do not exist, since it is so when awake, why does one not know it for oneself?
Since one does not even know for oneself that the objects of perception are non-existent, how could it be the case that, like dream-consciousness, real objects are entirely absent?
This, too, is not a proof.
The verse says:
Before awakening one cannot know that what is seen in a dream does not exist;
the treatise says:
Just as in the state prior to awakening, one does not know that the objects of a dream are not externally real, but knows them only upon awakening.

Thus, the world is like a dream, conditioned by the habitual maturation of false conceptualization; whatever is perceived therein does not truly exist, yet because true awakening has not been attained, one cannot know this for oneself.
When one attains that supramundane, non-conceptual wisdom which serves as the antidote, it is then termed "true awakening.
Subsequently, when the purified mundane wisdom attained thereafter manifests, one realizes, in accordance with reality, that those objects are not real; their meaning is thus equalized.

If sentient beings give rise to consciousness that appears as objects through the specific transformations within their own mental continuums, rather than arising with external objects as its objective referents, then those sentient beings' two types of consciousness—those hearing the correct Dharma and those hearing the false Dharma—are determined by whether they associate closely with virtuous or non-virtuous friends.
Since there is no instruction from a friend, how can this be established?
It is not that it cannot be established.
The verse says:
Through the successive force of mutual predominance, two consciousnesses become determinate.
The commentary states:

Because the various consciousnesses within the continuums of self and others among all sentient beings serve as mutually predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), two consciousnesses become determinate according to their respective circumstances. That is to say, due to the differentiation of consciousness in one continuum, it causes the production of differentiated consciousness in another continuum; each thus becomes determinate without depending on external objects.

If, as in a dream, consciousness arises even though its objects lack reality, then the consciousness of the waking state is likewise so; for what reason, then, do the wholesome and unwholesome deeds performed in dreams and the waking state result in different agreeable or disagreeable fruits that one must experience?
The verse says:
The mind is impaired by sleep; the results of dreaming and waking differ.
The commentary says:
In the state of dreaming, the mind is impaired by sleep and its power is weak; the waking mind is not so.
Therefore, regarding the karmic formations one performs that lead to the experience of maturation, the difference between superior and inferior results does not arise from external objects.
If there were only consciousness and no body, speech, or other such factors, how could sheep and the like be killed by others?
If the death of sheep and the like does not result from harm inflicted by another, how can the butcher incur the transgression of taking life?
The verse says:
Through the transformation of another’s consciousness, there occurs the act of killing;
as by the power of the minds of spirits and the like, others are made to lose mindfulness and so forth.
The treatise says:

Just as through the power of the mental intentions of spirits and the like, other sentient beings lose mindfulness and experience dreams, or undergo transformations such as being possessed by demons and so forth.

Those possessed of supernormal powers (abhijñā) can, through the power of their mental intention, cause others to see various things within their dreams; for example, by the power of Mahākātyāyana’s volition, he caused King Śreṇika and others to see extraordinary events in their dreams.
Furthermore, it is like the power of the mental indignation of a forest-dwelling rishi, which caused King Vemacitra to see strange things in a dream.
In this same way, due to the transformation of another's consciousness, an event occurs that violates and harms the life-faculty of another.
One should understand that "death" refers to the cessation of the continuum of the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings) due to the transformation of consciousness.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"How can the *tāṇḍaka* trees and others become empty through the wrath of a seer?"
"Mental punishment is a great sin; how can this be established?
The treatise says:

If it were not admitted that the death of another sentient being occurs through the dominant influence of the transformation of one's own consciousness, how could the Blessed One, in order to establish that mental punishment is a great sin, have posed a counter-question to the householder Upāli?
“Have you ever heard for what reason the Daṇḍaka forest, the Matanga forest, and the Kaliṅga forest have all become empty, desolate, and silent?
The householder addressed the Buddha, saying: “Gautama!”
"I have heard that it was due to the sage’s mental indignation.

If you maintain that gods and spirits, out of reverence for the sage, know his aversion and kill those sentient beings, then how can you cite that case to establish that mental punishment (*manodaṇḍa*) is a transgression of a greater sinful nature than that of body or speech? It would not be solely due to the sage’s mental indignation.
From this it should be understood that the principle—that those sentient beings die solely due to the wrath of the rishis—is well-established.
If there is only consciousness, do those who possess the knowledge of others' minds know the minds of others?
If this were the case, what fault would there be?
If one cannot know [the minds of others], how can it be called "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*)?
If one can know them, then the doctrine of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) should not be established.
Although one knows the minds of others, it is not according to reality.
The verse says:
How is it that the knowledge of others' minds knows its object as it truly is?
"Just as one knows the mind of another, one does not know it as it truly is, such as the realm of a Buddha.
The commentary says:
Why do those who possess the knowledge of others' minds not know their objects as they truly are?
Regarding the mind that knows itself:
how could this self-knowing mind not know its object as it truly is?
It is because of ignorance.

Because these two types of knowledge are each obscured by ignorance regarding their respective objects, they do not know the ineffable realm that is the sphere of activity of the Buddha’s pure knowledge.
These two do not know their objects as they truly are, because objects appear falsely as if they were external and because the discrimination between the grasped and the grasper has not been severed.

The systematic determination of the principles of Consciousness-Only is boundless; its various categories and distinctions are difficult to fathom and profoundly deep. Who but a Buddha could provide a comprehensive and extensive determination?
The verse says:
Having followed my own ability, I have briefly established the meaning of Consciousness-Only.
"Herein, every aspect is the inconceivable conduct of the Buddha.
The Commentary says:
The categories of the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) are boundless; I have established them briefly according to my own ability.
All other aspects are beyond the scope of deliberation, for they transcend the domain of discursive thought.
Such a principle is the exclusive province of the Buddhas, because the Buddha-Bhagavāns possess unimpeded knowledge regarding all objects and in all their modes.
*Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, One Fascicle.
